newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - Bond vols slide as Fed finally makes move.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Bond vols slide as Fed finally makes move.

text.p: Implied volatility of bond options on LIFFE tumbled on Wednesday after the U.S. raised interest rates, erasing weeks of uncertainty over U.S. monetary policy, brokers said.

"Volatility is getting sold big time," said a trader at a French brokerage in London. "Uncertainty over U.S. interest rates has disappeared in a puff of smoke and we've now got a four day drop in time decay."
He said volatiltiy of Bund, gilt and BTP options had all slid since Tuesday after the U.S. Federal Reserve raised its federal funds rate to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent.
A broker at another French house in London added about Bunds, "Unsurprisingly the May volatility has taken a tumble with the future behaving itself."
Brokers quoted implied volatility of the June 100.50 Bund straddle at 5.50 percent down from 5.73 percent at the close on Tuesday.
Implied volatility of June gilts was quoted at 7.80 percent compared with 8.15 percent at the opening on Wednesday while June BTP volatility was down 60 basis points to 8.10 percent, brokers said.
Debt futures on LIFFE held up fairly well to the widely flagged fed funds rise.
At 1455 GMT, June Bunds were off 0.26 at 100.21, June gilts were down 9/32 at 109-08 and June BTPs were up 0.19 at 125.40. On the MATIF, the notionnel were up 0.08 at 128.18.

In the U.S., June T-bond futures were down 9/32, at 108-10, broadsided by stronger-than-expected durable goods orders. Orders climbed 1.5 percent in February to a seasonally adjusted record of $178.3 billion compared with expectations for a 0.4 percent drop.
Pure volatility plays were the order of the day, said the trader at the first French house.
"There hasn't been one voltility buying strategy, they have all been selling, straddles, strangles," he said.
Traders said 6,000 lots of May 101.50 Bund calls had changed hands.
"Everyone's had a nibble at those things," the second French broker said. "They're looking cheap because of the volatility and the time decay."
Most of Europe have Friday and Monday off for Easter.
